segment:
“It is a glass of wine,” he said, looking at Mara. “An ordinary plastic cup, such as is now being handed out by that woman, carrying wine in it. If you see anything different, you may certainly tell us.” His gaze still on hers, he placed his right hand flat against the table beside them and said to Jonah, “Hold this, will you?”
Jonah picked up the cup. “Do I want the contents first?”
Adrian waved that aside. “We won’t break the cup, don’t worry.” He held up his left hand, palm outward, toward Mara, and placed three objects in her open palm: a brass key, a white stone, and a wooden token.
Mara looked down at his hand, then up into his eyes, waiting to see what was wanted next.
“Choose one of those three,” he said. “Silently, please. Which one will you keep?” He smiled, leaned closer, and said, “You don’t have to answer right now, mind; but if you don’t want to play at all, we should stop.”

Next manuscript lines after the continuation
Her eyes locked with his as she said, “I think I would rather play than not,” and let her eyes fall to her palm, where she had three objects laid out. She closed her left hand around two of them and opened it again with only the brass key remaining in her palm. She turned her hand face down, keeping the brass key against her palm and the other side of her hand facing the group as she looked back up into Adrian’s eyes and nodded.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

segment:
The older woman had brought the young man his glass, then taken it back after he drank from it. That was a job, and someone would pay her for it. This was what they’d done with money over generations: they paid women to clean up after men and children, and then the next generation considered it natural that some women always knew where the trash belonged.
A third voice came out of the hallway now, loud and clear; and Mara realized it was hers, and someone was answering it.
Someone named Adrian.

Manchu script
First part

She was standing stock-still with her eyes fixed on the woman when she heard him say her name. She startled a little and turned around, to find him smiling at her. His face looked younger than his body’s size had made it seem, but there was a smile on it now where he hadn’t smiled before. He looked her over with slow curiosity and said, “Are you looking forward to meeting the Reader?”
“I haven’t met anyone else yet either.” And this wasn’t exactly true, though she wouldn’t admit how close to true it was.
“Yes,” Adrian replied, nodding very seriously, “I have noticed that I too haven’t met anyone yet. Let me introduce you.”

As he spoke, someone else appeared in the hallway behind Mara’s shoulders. She turned to look and found her original blonde man, Jonah, standing there with his own glass of wine.
“I thought it was your turn,” he remarked, watching Adrian move forward.
“Well,” said Adrian, “not yet, no. In fact, I wasn’t quite finished.”

segment:
It was a useful observation; and then it was over. But Mara had nothing to say about it, so she just kept watching, waiting, not moving. She didn’t even know whose labor was assumed by whom.
Then there were more people in the hall behind them—another woman’s voice and a male voice. A blonde woman entered with the same dark-framed glasses that Jonah had been wearing. The man had shorter black hair, but both of them nodded at Jonah as they came in; they did not seem to notice Mara at all.

They were not speaking aloud, but the woman made a gesture toward the table by the door—and in response, Jonah put his right hand on Mara’s shoulder and walked her over to the table. He introduced Mara to Adrian and Rue with an obvious level of familiarity that he had not extended to Mara yet: “This is my friend Mara. I met her today while she was doing interviews.”
And then, like a conductor leading the group into a new section of music, Jonah raised both arms in front of his chest as if holding someone back from them and spoke to Adrian:
“She’s a really good guesser,” Jonah said, turning to address Mara again with his face while keeping the gesture of his arms still pointed away. “Do you remember the last time she surprised us?”

Mara smiled awkwardly, looking from Jonah to Adrian, and then saw her opening to take charge. She stepped forward, still standing behind Jonah as he blocked the other two people out with his arms.
